questions.stem_md: A zero-order reaction has $k = 0.005\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\ \text{s}^{-1}$. How long, in seconds, does the reactant take to fall from $0.80$ to $0.30\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$?

A pesticide washed into a pond breaks down by a first-order process with a half-life of 4 days. What fraction of it remains after 12 days, and why does the half-life not depend on how much pesticide entered the pond?

answer.model_answer_md: Twelve days is three half-lives, so the fraction left is (1/2)³ = 1/8, or 12.5%. For a first-order process t½ = 0.693/k contains no concentration term, so every halving takes 4 days whatever the starting amount.

questions.solution_md: Count half-lives; first-order half-life is independent of concentration.

questions.stem_md: Starting from the integrated rate equation $k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\ce{R}]_0}{[\ce{R}]}$, show that the half-life of a first-order reaction is $\dfrac{0.693}{k}$. Hence explain why it is independent of the initial concentration.

answer.model_answer_md:
At $t = t_{1/2}$, $[\ce{R}] = \dfrac{[\ce{R}]_0}{2}$, so $\dfrac{[\ce{R}]_0}{[\ce{R}]} = 2$.

$k = \dfrac{2.303}{t_{1/2}}\log 2 = \dfrac{2.303 \times 0.3010}{t_{1/2}}$, so $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}$.

The expression contains only $k$ and no concentration term, so the half-life is the same whatever the starting concentration.

questions.solution_md: Substitute [R] = [R]₀/2 and log 2 = 0.3010.

questions.stem_md: What is a pseudo-first-order reaction? Write the rate expression for the acid-catalysed inversion of cane sugar and explain why it behaves as first order.

answer.model_answer_md: A pseudo-first-order reaction is one whose true order is higher, but which behaves as first order because one reactant is present in large excess. In the inversion of cane sugar, $\ce{C12H22O11 + H2O ->[H+] C6H12O6 + C6H12O6}$, the true rate is $k[\text{sucrose}][\ce{H2O}]$. Water is the solvent and in huge excess, so its concentration hardly changes and $k[\ce{H2O}] = k'$; the rate becomes $k'[\text{sucrose}]$, first order in sucrose.

questions.solution_md: Definition, rate expression, and why the excess reactant is absorbed into k′.

marking_scheme.step: Balanced reaction and true rate law
Water in excess, so rate = k′[sucrose]

questions.stem_md: In two experiments on the same reaction at the same temperature, the half-life was 20 min when the initial concentration was 0.80 mol L⁻¹, and 10 min when it was 0.40 mol L⁻¹. (a) What is the order of the reaction? Justify. (b) Calculate the rate constant with its unit. (c) How long will the 0.80 mol L⁻¹ solution take to react completely?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The half-life is directly proportional to the initial concentration (halving $[\ce{R}]_0$ halves $t_{1/2}$), so the reaction is **zero order**.

(b) $k = \dfrac{[\ce{R}]_0}{2t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.80}{2 \times 20} = 0.02\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\ \text{min}^{-1}$.

(c) $t = \dfrac{[\ce{R}]_0}{k} = \dfrac{0.80}{0.02} = 40\ \text{min}$.

questions.solution_md: Proportional half-life means zero order; use t½ = [R]₀/2k.

questions.stem_md: A catalyst increases the rate of a reversible reaction. Which quantity does it change?

options.text_md: The enthalpy change of the reaction
The equilibrium constant
The Gibbs energy change of the reaction
The activation energy

questions.solution_md: A catalyst offers a different path with a lower activation energy; the energies of reactants and products, and hence ΔH, ΔG and K, are unchanged — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A graph of $\ln k$ against $\dfrac{1}{T}$ for a reaction is a straight line. Its slope equals:

options.text_md: $\dfrac{E_\text{a}}{R}$
$-\dfrac{E_\text{a}}{2.303R}$
$-\dfrac{E_\text{a}}{R}$
$\ln A$

questions.solution_md: $\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_\text{a}}{R}\cdot\dfrac{1}{T}$, so the slope is $-\dfrac{E_\text{a}}{R}$ and the intercept is $\ln A$ — option (c). (b) is the slope of the $\log k$ plot.

questions.stem_md: A reaction has a temperature coefficient of 2 (its rate doubles for every 10 K rise). By what factor does the rate increase when the temperature rises from 300 K to 340 K?
questions.solution_md: A 40 K rise is four 10 K steps: $2^4 = 16$ — option (b). (a) uses three steps; (d) multiplies instead of using powers.

questions.stem_md: Reactions P and Q have activation energies of 40 and 120 kJ mol⁻¹. When both are warmed by the same few kelvin, which statement is correct?

options.text_md: The rate of P increases by a larger factor than the rate of Q.
Both rates increase by the same factor.
The rate of Q increases by a larger factor than the rate of P.
Neither rate changes, because Ea does not depend on temperature.

questions.solution_md: $\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_\text{a}}{2.303R}\left(\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1T_2}\right)$ is proportional to $E_\text{a}$, so the reaction with the larger activation energy is more sensitive to temperature — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** For many reactions, the rate roughly doubles when the temperature is raised by 10 K.

**Reason (R):** The total number of collisions per second doubles when the temperature is raised by 10 K.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: a 10 K rise increases the collision frequency by only a few per cent; the rate doubles because the fraction of molecules with energy at least Ea roughly doubles — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction by lowering its activation energy.

**Reason (R):** A catalyst makes the Gibbs energy change of the reaction more negative.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: a catalyst does not change ΔG (or ΔH or K); it only provides a path with lower Ea — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The unstable, highest-energy arrangement of atoms formed when reactant molecules pass over the energy barrier is called the activated ___.
questions.solution_md: It is the activated **complex** (transition state).

questions.stem_md: The rate constant of a reaction doubles when the temperature is raised from $300\ \text{K}$ to $310\ \text{K}$. Calculate the activation energy in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. ($R = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$, $\log 2 = 0.3010$)
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — $\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_\text{a}}{2.303R}\left(\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1T_2}\right)$, so $E_\text{a} = \dfrac{2.303R\,T_1T_2\log 2}{T_2 - T_1}$.

Step 2 — $E_\text{a} = \dfrac{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 300 \times 310 \times 0.3010}{10} \approx 53\,600$ J $\text{mol}^{-1}$.

Step 3 — In kilojoules: $E_\text{a} = 53600 \div 1000 = 53.6$, so about $53.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

marking_scheme.step: Substitution with T in K and R in J

questions.stem_md: The rate constant of a gas-phase reaction is $0.020\ \text{s}^{-1}$ at $500\ \text{K}$ and $0.070\ \text{s}^{-1}$ at $700\ \text{K}$. Calculate $E_\text{a}$ in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. ($R = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$, $\log 3.5 = 0.544$)
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — $\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{0.070}{0.020} = 3.5$.

Step 2 — $E_\text{a} = \dfrac{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 500 \times 700 \times 0.544}{200} \approx 18\,200$ J $\text{mol}^{-1}$; in kilojoules $18200 \div 1000 = 18.2$, so about $18.2\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: State the effect of a catalyst on (a) the activation energy, (b) the enthalpy change and (c) the equilibrium constant of a reaction. Explain your answer to (c).

answer.model_answer_md: (a) It lowers the activation energy. (b) It has no effect on the enthalpy change. (c) It has no effect on the equilibrium constant, because it lowers the barrier equally for the forward and the backward reactions, so both speed up by the same factor and equilibrium is only reached sooner.

questions.solution_md: Lower Ea; ΔH and K unchanged; forward and backward rates rise equally.

marking_scheme.step: (c) K unchanged because both directions speed up equally

questions.stem_md: A reaction has $E_\text{a} = 60\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $k = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ at $300\ \text{K}$. Calculate $k$ at $320\ \text{K}$. ($R = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$)

answer.model_answer_md:
$\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{60000}{2.303 \times 8.314}\left(\dfrac{320 - 300}{300 \times 320}\right) \approx 3134 \times 2.083 \times 10^{-4} \approx 0.653$.

$\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} \approx 10^{0.653} \approx 4.50$.

$k_2 \approx 4.50 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-3} \approx 9.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: Ea in joules, T in kelvin; then antilog.

marking_scheme.step: Correct substitution with Ea in J

questions.stem_md: Most collisions between reactant molecules do not lead to a reaction because:

options.text_md: molecules in a gas never really touch each other
collisions only happen at high temperature
every collision needs a catalyst to be effective
they lack the threshold energy or the proper orientation

questions.solution_md: An effective collision needs energy at least equal to the threshold energy and the correct orientation; most collisions fail one of these — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In the collision theory expression rate $= P\,Z_\text{AB}\,e^{-E_\text{a}/RT}$, the factor $P$ allows for:

options.text_md: the number of collisions per second per unit volume
the fraction of molecules with energy at least Ea
the fraction of collisions in which the molecules are suitably oriented
the pressure of the reacting gases

questions.solution_md: $Z_\text{AB}$ is the collision frequency (a), $e^{-E_\text{a}/RT}$ the energetic fraction (b), and $P$ the probability (steric) factor for proper orientation — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Every collision in which the molecules have energy greater than the threshold energy leads to products.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The molecules must also collide with the proper orientation.

questions.stem_md: Using collision theory, explain why raising the temperature increases the rate of a reaction much more than it increases the number of collisions per second.

answer.model_answer_md: A small rise in temperature increases the collision frequency only slightly, but it greatly increases the fraction of molecules having energy at least equal to the threshold energy. Since only such energetic, properly oriented collisions are effective, the number of effective collisions, and so the rate, rises sharply.

questions.solution_md: Distinguish collision frequency from the fraction of energetic collisions.

marking_scheme.step: Fraction of collisions with energy ≥ threshold rises greatly

questions.stem_md: Match each straight-line plot with what it shows.

options.text_md: [R] against t
log [R] against t
ln k against 1/T
log k against 1/T

questions.solution_md: Zero order is linear in [R]; first order is linear in log [R]; the Arrhenius plots are linear in 1/T, with slope −Ea/R for ln k and −Ea/2.303R for log k.

questions.stem_md: Ammonia decomposes on a hot platinum wire. At high pressure the rate stays constant while ammonia is used up, but at very low pressure the rate becomes proportional to the pressure of ammonia. Explain both observations.

answer.model_answer_md: At high pressure the platinum surface is completely covered with ammonia molecules, so extra gas cannot react any faster: the rate is constant, a zero-order reaction. At very low pressure only part of the surface is covered, and the number of adsorbed molecules, and so the rate, is proportional to the pressure: first order.

questions.solution_md: Surface saturated: zero order. Surface partly covered: rate proportional to pressure.

marking_scheme.step: High pressure: surface saturated, rate constant (zero order)
Low pressure: coverage ∝ pressure, so first order

questions.stem_md: A first-order reaction is 75% complete in 30 min. Find its half-life in minutes.
questions.solution_md: 75% complete leaves $\dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2^2}$ of the reactant, which is two half-lives. So $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{30}{2} = 15$, that is $15\ \text{min}$.

questions.stem_md: A first-order reaction is 20% complete in $10\ \text{min}$. Calculate its rate constant in $\text{min}^{-1}$. ($\log 1.25 = 0.0969$)
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — 20% complete leaves $[\ce{R}] = 0.8[\ce{R}]_0$, so $\dfrac{[\ce{R}]_0}{[\ce{R}]} = \dfrac{1}{0.8} = 1.25$.

Step 2 — $k = \dfrac{2.303}{10} \times 0.0969 \approx 0.0223$, in $\text{min}^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: A plot of $\log k$ against $\dfrac{1}{T}$ for a reaction is a straight line of slope $-2000\ \text{K}$. The activation energy is ($R = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$):

options.text_md: about $38.3\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$
about $16.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$
about $2.0\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$
about $4.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

questions.solution_md: Slope $= -\dfrac{E_\text{a}}{2.303R}$, so $E_\text{a} = 2000 \times 2.303 \times 8.314 \approx 38\,300$ J $\text{mol}^{-1}$ — option (a). (b) treats the line as $\ln k$ against $1/T$ (slope $-E_\text{a}/R$); (c) reads the slope as the energy itself.

questions.stem_md: The total pressure of a gaseous reaction mixture is doubled at constant temperature by compressing it. The rate increases mainly because:

options.text_md: a larger fraction of molecules now has energy above the activation energy
the activation energy is lowered by compression
the rate constant increases with pressure
the molecules are closer together, so they collide more often

questions.solution_md: Compression raises concentrations and so the collision frequency; at constant temperature the energy distribution, Ea and k are unchanged — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
(a) Derive the integrated rate equation for a first-order reaction, $k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\ce{R}]_0}{[\ce{R}]}$.

(b) The gas-phase decomposition $\mathrm{A(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{B(g)} + \mathrm{C(g)}$ is first order. Starting with pure A at $0.40\ \text{atm}$, the total pressure after $100\ \text{s}$ is $0.60\ \text{atm}$ at constant volume and temperature. Calculate $k$ and the half-life.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) For $\mathrm{R} \rightarrow \mathrm{P}$, $-\dfrac{d[\ce{R}]}{dt} = k[\ce{R}]$, so $\dfrac{d[\ce{R}]}{[\ce{R}]} = -k\,dt$. Integrating, $\ln[\ce{R}] = -kt + I$; at $t = 0$, $I = \ln[\ce{R}]_0$. So $\ln\dfrac{[\ce{R}]_0}{[\ce{R}]} = kt$, and converting to common logarithms, $k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\ce{R}]_0}{[\ce{R}]}$.

(b) If A falls by $x$, total pressure $= 0.40 + x = 0.60$, so $x = 0.20$ and $p_\text{A} = 0.20\ \text{atm}$. $k = \dfrac{2.303}{100}\log\dfrac{0.40}{0.20} = 0.02303 \times 0.3010 \approx 6.93 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}$. $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{6.93 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 100\ \text{s}$ — consistent, since A halved in 100 s.

questions.solution_md: Separate variables and integrate; for the gas, find the partial pressure of A from the total pressure.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Rate law and separation of variables
(a) Integration with the constant from t = 0
(b) p(A) = 0.20 atm from the total pressure

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write the integrated rate equations and half-life expressions for zero- and first-order reactions, and sketch the straight-line plot for each.

(b) Two reactions start with $[\ce{R}]_0 = 1.0\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ and the same initial rate of $0.10\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\ \text{min}^{-1}$; one is zero order, the other first order. Find the half-life of each and the time each takes to reach 75% completion. Comment on the difference.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Zero order: $[\ce{R}] = [\ce{R}]_0 - kt$; $[\ce{R}]$ vs $t$ is a straight line of slope $-k$; $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[\ce{R}]_0}{2k}$. First order: $\log[\ce{R}] = \log[\ce{R}]_0 - \dfrac{kt}{2.303}$; $\log[\ce{R}]$ vs $t$ is a straight line of slope $-k/2.303$; $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}$.

(b) Zero order: $k = 0.10\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\ \text{min}^{-1}$, $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{1.0}{0.20} = 5$ min; 75% means 0.75 mol L⁻¹ used: $t = \dfrac{0.75}{0.10} = 7.5$ min. First order: rate $= k[\ce{R}]_0$ gives $k = 0.10\ \text{min}^{-1}$, $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.10} = 6.93$ min; 75% is two half-lives, about 13.9 min. The first-order reaction slows as the reactant is used, so it takes longer, whereas the zero-order one keeps a constant rate.

questions.solution_md: Same starting rate fixes k for each order; compare times.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Comment on why first order is slower later

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define rate law, order and molecularity. Why can the order of a reaction not be predicted from its balanced equation?

(b) For $\ce{A + 2B -> products}$ at a fixed temperature:

| Run | $[\ce{A}]$ / M | $[\ce{B}]$ / M | Initial rate / M s⁻¹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.10 | 0.20 | $3.0 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| 2 | 0.30 | 0.20 | $2.7 \times 10^{-3}$ |
| 3 | 0.10 | 0.40 | $3.0 \times 10^{-4}$ |

Find the order in each reactant, the rate law and the rate constant with its unit.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The rate law expresses the rate in terms of reactant concentrations raised to experimentally found powers; order is the sum of these powers; molecularity is the number of species colliding in an elementary step. Most reactions happen in several steps, and the rate depends on the slowest step, not on the overall equation, so the order must be found by experiment.

(b) Runs 1, 2: [A] ×3, rate ×9, so second order in A. Runs 1, 3: [B] ×2, rate unchanged, so zero order in B. Rate $= k[\ce{A}]^2$. $k = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{-4}}{0.10^2} = 0.03\ \text{L mol}^{-1}\ \text{s}^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: Definitions and the mechanism argument; compare runs for each reactant.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Reason: mechanism / slowest step, found by experiment
(b) Rate law and k = 0.03 L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write the Arrhenius equation and explain the meaning of each term.

(b) Draw an energy profile for an exothermic reaction with and without a catalyst, labelling the activation energies and ΔH.

(c) A reaction has $E_\text{a} = 50\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. At what temperature will its rate constant be four times its value at $300\ \text{K}$? ($R = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$, $\log 4 = 0.602$)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $k = Ae^{-E_\text{a}/RT}$: $k$ is the rate constant, $A$ the frequency (pre-exponential) factor, $E_\text{a}$ the activation energy, $R$ the gas constant and $T$ the temperature in kelvin; $e^{-E_\text{a}/RT}$ is the fraction of molecules with energy at least $E_\text{a}$.

(b) Energy against reaction coordinate: reactants at a higher level than products; a tall hump (uncatalysed) and a lower hump (catalysed) between them; $E_\text{a}$ measured from the reactants to each peak; ΔH from reactants down to products, the same for both paths.

(c) $\log 4 = \dfrac{50000}{2.303 \times 8.314}\left(\dfrac{1}{300} - \dfrac{1}{T_2}\right)$, so $\dfrac{1}{300} - \dfrac{1}{T_2} \approx \dfrac{0.602 \times 19.15}{50000} \approx 2.31 \times 10^{-4}$. $\dfrac{1}{T_2} \approx 3.333 \times 10^{-3} - 0.231 \times 10^{-3} \approx 3.103 \times 10^{-3}$, so $T_2 \approx 322\ \text{K}$.

questions.solution_md: Rearrange the two-temperature form for 1/T₂.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Profile with both humps, Ea and ΔH labelled

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the main postulates of collision theory, including the role of the threshold energy and orientation.

(b) Use a sketch of the distribution of molecular energies at two temperatures to explain why a small rise in temperature greatly increases the rate.

(c) Explain, using the same ideas, how a catalyst increases the rate. State one limitation of collision theory.

answer.model_answer_md: Reactant molecules are treated as hard spheres, and a reaction occurs only when they collide. Only effective collisions, with energy at least equal to the threshold energy and with the proper orientation, give products; rate = P Z e^(−Ea/RT). A sketch of the energy distribution shows that at the higher temperature the curve flattens and shifts to higher energies, so the area beyond the activation energy, the fraction of molecules able to react, increases greatly, roughly doubling for a 10 K rise, while the collision frequency hardly changes. A catalyst provides a path of lower activation energy; the Ea line moves left, so a much larger fraction of collisions is effective at the same temperature. A limitation is that molecules are treated as structureless spheres, so the steric factor has to be introduced empirically.

questions.solution_md: Postulates, energy distribution argument, catalyst moving the Ea line, one limitation.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Sketch with two curves and Ea line
(c) Catalyst lowers Ea, larger fraction effective

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md: A dairy cooperative in Anand tests how long fresh milk takes to turn sour. Stored in a refrigerator at 278 K, a sample takes about 64 hours; on a kitchen shelf at 303 K, an identical sample takes about 4 hours. Souring is caused by bacterial enzymes that convert lactose into lactic acid. Assume that the time taken is inversely proportional to the rate constant.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (b) A larger fraction of reacting molecules has energy at least equal to the activation energy at 303 K.

**(b)** 16

**(c)** (i) $E_\text{a} = \dfrac{2.303R\,T_1T_2\log 16}{T_2 - T_1} = \dfrac{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 278 \times 303 \times 1.204}{25} \approx 77\,700\ \text{J mol}^{-1}$, about $77.7\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

**OR** (ii) The statement is wrong. In the refrigerator the milk still sours, but after about 64 hours instead of 4: cooling lowers the fraction of molecules with energy above the activation energy, so the rate falls about 16 times, but it does not become zero.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Ea itself does not change with temperature; warming raises the fraction of molecules with enough energy, so the rate constant increases — option (b).

**(b)** Rate $\propto \dfrac{1}{\text{time}}$, so the ratio $= \dfrac{64}{4} = 16$.

**(c)** (i) Two-temperature Arrhenius equation with the rate ratio from (b).

(ii) Use the 64 h figure: the reaction slows but continues.

children.stem_md: Which statement best explains why the milk sours faster on the shelf?

options.text_md: The activation energy of the reaction is lower at 303 K.
A larger fraction of reacting molecules has energy at least equal to the activation energy at 303 K.
The enzymes are destroyed at the lower temperature.
The equilibrium constant of souring is larger in the refrigerator.

questions.passage_md: A car’s catalytic converter contains a honeycomb coated with a thin layer of platinum and rhodium. It speeds up reactions that turn carbon monoxide and unburnt hydrocarbons into carbon dioxide and water, and nitrogen oxides into nitrogen. Mechanics in Pune note that the converter does little during the first minute after a cold start, but works well once it is above about 500 K.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (c) It provides a reaction path with a lower activation energy.

**(b)** It gives a very large surface area of catalyst, so more gas molecules can react on it each second.

**(c)** (i) Even with the catalyst, the reactions still have an activation energy. At a low temperature only a tiny fraction of gas molecules have enough energy to react on the surface, so the rate is very small. As the converter warms above about 500 K, this fraction grows sharply and the reactions become fast.

**OR** (ii) The claim is wrong. A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally and does not change the equilibrium constant. It only helps the gases reach the equilibrium mixture, which already strongly favours carbon dioxide, during the short time they spend in the converter.

**(b)** Surface area.

**(c)** (i) A lowered Ea is still an Ea; the energetic fraction depends on temperature.

(ii) Catalysts change rates, not equilibrium positions.
